content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
C++ is a general-purpose, compiled, statically typed language that combines low-level control with abstraction. Start with standard C++ and use an explicit compiler mode rather than relying on an implementation default.

Introduction to C++ focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check. One wording correction is important: C++ is not an acronym; the name alludes to the C increment operator.

Confirm that the compiler is installed, compile a small `.cpp` file, run it, and make one deliberate change to see the edit-build-run cycle.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Introduction to C++
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.

items.title: What Is C++?
items.text: Define C++ in plain language, connect it to Introduction to C++, and identify where it appears in a real C++ program.

items.title: What Does C++ Stand For?
items.text: C++ is a name built from the C language and the increment operator; it is not an acronym with an official expanded phrase.

items.title: The Purpose of C++
items.text: Explain the purpose of c++ with its language-standard context and verify implementation support rather than assuming every compiler behaves identically.

items.title: Key Characteristics of C++
items.text: Explain key characteristics of c++ with its language-standard context and verify implementation support rather than assuming every compiler behaves identically.

items.title: C++ as a Compiled Language
items.text: A C++ implementation translates source through a toolchain into object code and a linked executable or library; build steps can be separate.

items.title: C++ as a Statically Typed Language
items.text: Types are checked through declarations and type deduction; the compiler diagnoses many incompatible operations before a program runs.

items.title: The Relationship Between C and C++
items.text: Explain the relationship between c and c++ with its language-standard context and verify implementation support rather than assuming every compiler behaves identically.

items.title: C++ and Other Programming Languages
items.text: Explain c++ and other programming languages with its language-standard context and verify implementation support rather than assuming every compiler behaves identically.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate what is c++?, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: Use standard C++ rather than compiler-specific behavior unless the lesson explicitly labels the dependency. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

content.task: Create a small, independent example that demonstrates introduction to c++. Predict the result before compiling, write down a precondition, and test one ordinary case plus one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example builds under a documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted and observed result are recorded; deviations are explained.
At least one boundary, invalid-input, lifetime or portability assumption is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the smallest example that demonstrates what is c++?.
Trace the relevant values and state the expected output before running the program.
Check the standard/compiler reference and add an edge case instead of relying only on the happy path.
summary: Introduction to C++ is about a concrete language rule or engineering decision, not only terminology.
Keep the important preconditions and trade-offs visible when applying introduction to c++.
Use explicit build settings and focused tests to support the claim that the example behaves as expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
